t: Maximize Number of Nice Divisors: Prime Exponents Meet the Integer Break
o: Write n as a product of primes p_1^e_1 * p_2^e_2 * ... A divisor is nice when every distinct prime of n divides it, which forces it to use exponent f_i between 0 and e_i for each prime independently — so the count of nice divisors equals e_1 * e_2 * ... * e_k, the product of the exponents. The budget is primeFactors = sum of exponents, and using fewer than all of it never helps since raising any exponent only multiplies the product. Hence we must split the integer primeFactors into positive parts maximizing their product: 5 becomes 3 + 2 with product 6 (Example 1), and 8 becomes 3 + 3 + 2 with product 18 (Example 2). Parts of 3 dominate — three 2s lose to two 3s because 8 < 9 — a leftover 1 merges into a neighbor, and at most two 2s should ever appear. With primeFactors up to 10^9, the answer is computed as modular powers via fast exponentiation rather than any linear loop.
k: Nice divisors of n = product p_i^{e_i} number exactly product e_i, so the problem reduces to pure exponent budgeting.
Maximizing a product under a fixed sum favors 3s: replace 2+2+2 by 3+3 (gain), avoid parts of 1 entirely, and keep at most two 2s in an optimal split.
primeFactors up to 10^9 demands O(log k) modular fast exponentiation; multiplying in a loop or DP over the budget cannot finish.
Handle tiny budgets separately: for primeFactors <= 3 the answer is primeFactors itself.

a.i: Define dp[x] as the maximum product obtainable from budget x, combining a first part j with the optimal split dp[x - j]; dp[0] = 1 seeds empty splits. This is exact and easy to verify on small inputs, but quadratic time and linear memory confine it to budgets of a few thousand at best — included to motivate the closed-form greedy that follows.
s: For each x from 1 to primeFactors, set dp[x] = max over j of j * dp[x - j].
a.t: O(k^2) time and O(k) space for budget k — exact but hopeless once k approaches 10^9; useful only as intuition on small cases.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy Threes with Fast Modular Exponentiation
a.i: An optimal split uses as many 3s as possible. Let q and r be the quotient and remainder of primeFactors divided by 3: r = 0 gives 3^q; r = 1 wastes a unit (3+1 < 2+2), so regroup into one 4 plus q - 1 threes, yielding 4 * 3^(q-1); r = 2 appends a single 2, giving 2 * 3^q. Budgets of 1, 2, 3 are answered directly. Each case reduces to computing 3^q modulo 10^9 + 7 through binary exponentiation, which needs only about 30 squarings even for q near 333 million.
s: Compute q = primeFactors / 3 and r = primeFactors % 3.
r == 0: return pow(3, q) mod M.
r == 1: return 4 * pow(3, q - 1) mod M; otherwise return 2 * pow(3, q) mod M.
Implement the power by repeated squaring with modular reduction at every step.
a.t: O(log k) — binary exponentiation performs O(log k) multiplications on machine-size residues.
a.sp: O(1) — a handful of numeric variables.

w: Recognizing the reduction nice-divisors-count = product-of-exponents is the heart of the problem; after that you are solving LC 343 (Integer Break) with modular arithmetic. In an interview, state the reduction, sketch why parts larger than 4 are suboptimal (split x into floor(x/2) * ceil(x/2) > x), then derive the three-way remainder formula before coding. Pitfalls: forgetting the primeFactors <= 3 special case (the remainder-1 branch indexes 3^(q-1) and breaks at q = 0), reducing only after multiplying huge values (overflow in fixed-width languages), and JavaScript precision loss when squaring numbers near 10^9 without BigInt. Follow-ups: construct an actual n achieving the optimum (assign exponents to arbitrary distinct primes), or handle queries asking for the answer over many budgets, which reuses the same O(log k) routine per query.
